opus-5.5.text:
I think the connection is less about specific knowledge and more about a way of thinking.

In undergrad I worked on theoretical physics, condensed matter and topological phases, problems where you try to find the simplest structure that explains a complicated phenomenon. What I took from that was a habit: when something looks messy, ask what the essential degrees of freedom are, what symmetry or principle is at work, and what the cleanest toy model is that still captures it. In physics you're trained not to be satisfied with "it works." You want to understand why it works and when it will stop working.

When I moved into AI, I found that habit useful, and sometimes I had to push against it. Modern AI research is much more empirical. A lot of progress comes from scaling things up, running experiments, and seeing what happens, often before anyone has a good theory. So part of the transition was accepting that the system is ahead of our understanding, and that taste in choosing which experiments to run matters as much as elegance.

Still, I think the physics mindset pays off in a few places. One is thinking in terms of scaling and emergence. Physicists are used to the idea that behavior at large scale can look qualitatively different from behavior at small scale, and that you can still find regularities, like scaling laws, in that change. Another is being comfortable with approximation: you don't need a complete theory to make good predictions, just the right approximation for the regime you care about.

So I'd say physics didn't give me the tools I use day to day in AI, but it shaped how I ask questions. I try to treat these models a bit like a new kind of physical system, something we built but don't fully understand, and that we can study with curiosity and rigor, the way you'd study nature.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI research as empirical and experiment driven, but it characterizes his undergraduate physics work as theoretical and does not say that both fields test ideas through computational experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that the connection is less about content and more about taste. Almost nothing I learned in condensed matter theory transfers directly. The math I use now is much simpler than what I did in physics, and the hard problems in AI right now are not really problems of theory in the physics sense.

What did transfer is a way of looking at a system and asking, what are the few things that actually matter here? In physics you are constantly trained to throw information away. You have a system with an astronomical number of degrees of freedom, and the whole game is finding the two or three effective variables that explain the behavior. When I look at a large model now, I have the same reflex. There is an enormous amount going on, and most of it is noise. The question is which quantities are the real order parameters, so to speak. Scaling laws are a very physics-flavored idea, for example. They are empirical, they are coarse, and they are powerful precisely because they ignore the details.

The other thing physics gave me is a certain comfort with not understanding. In my undergrad research I spent a long time on problems where nobody had a clean explanation, and you learn to work productively in that state. You make a conjecture, you poke at it with the cheapest experiment you can design, you update. That is basically what frontier AI research feels like day to day. People sometimes imagine it is very principled, and some of it is, but a lot of it is careful experimental science on an object we did not design in any detailed sense and do not fully understand. Physicists are comfortable with that. The universe did not give us a design document either.

I would also say physics made me a bit humble about the word "understanding." We had very successful theories of superconductivity for decades before anyone could say in a satisfying way why high temperature superconductors work, and in some sense we still cannot. So when people ask whether we understand these models, my instinct is to ask what level of description they want. We have very good predictive handles on some things and almost nothing on others, and that is a familiar situation to me.

If there is a loss, it is that physics has a kind of permanence I sometimes miss. A result in physics stays true. A lot of what I learn about today's models will be irrelevant in two years. But I came to feel that the questions in AI right now are simply more consequential for this particular moment in history, and I wanted to be close to them while the answers were still open. The physics training is what lets me be useful there. It is not what I work on, but it is how I think.

r001.rationale: The response says both fields involve forming conjectures and testing them with experiments, but it does not identify those experiments as computational.

astra-6.text:
I think the connection is mostly in how I approach problems. In physics, you try to find a simple model that captures the essential parts of something complicated. You make assumptions, derive consequences, and then ask whether the evidence supports them. That way of thinking is useful in AI, too: what is the underlying question, and what experiment would actually help us answer it?

But there’s also a difference. In physics, you’re trying to understand a world that already exists. In AI, you can build the system you’re studying, so understanding and invention are closely connected. You change something, observe its behavior, and use that to decide what to build next. So I see continuity in the scientific approach, even though the subject and the tools have changed.

r001.rationale: The response describes shared problem-solving and experimentation, including changing an AI system and observing its behavior, but does not clearly say that both physics and AI research test ideas through computational experiments.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the connection is less about a particular physics topic and more about a way of asking questions. In physics, you try to take a complicated phenomenon, identify the essential variables, and build a simple model that you can test. That way of thinking is useful in AI too: when a system succeeds or fails, what actually explains its behavior? What experiment would distinguish one explanation from another?

There’s also a difference. In physics, you’re trying to understand a world that already exists. In AI, you can change the system you’re studying. You build something, observe its behavior, and use that to decide what to build next. I find that combination of understanding and creating very appealing.

r001.rationale: The response describes a shared approach of testing models and using experiments to explain behavior, but it does not say those experiments are computational.
